{{short description|Positional numeral system}}
{{Numeral systems}}
In [[arithmetic]], a '''complex-base system''' is a [[positional numeral system]] whose [[radix]] is an [[imaginary number|imaginary]] (proposed by [[Donald Knuth]] in 1955<ref name="Knuth1">{{cite journal |last=Knuth |first=D.E. |title=An Imaginary Number System |journal=Communications of the ACM |year=1960 |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=245–247 |doi=10.1145/367177.367233|s2cid=16513137 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Knuth2">{{cite book |last=Knuth |first=Donald |authorlink=Donald Knuth |title=The art of computer programming |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Boston |year=1998 |volume=2 |edition=3rd |pages=205 |isbn=0-201-89684-2 |chapter=Positional Number Systems |oclc=48246681}}</ref>) or [[complex number]] (proposed by S. Khmelnik in 1964<ref name="Khmelnik1">{{cite journal |last=Khmelnik |first=S.I. |title=Specialized digital computer for operations with complex numbers
|journal=Questions of Radio Electronics (In Russian)|volume=XII |issue=2 |year=1964}}</ref> and Walter F. Penney in 1965<ref name="Penney0">W. Penney, A "binary" system for complex numbers, JACM 12 (1965) 247-248.</ref><ref name="Penney1">{{cite journal |last=Jamil |first=T. |year=2002 |title=The complex binary number system |journal=IEEE Potentials |volume=20 |pages=39–41 |doi=10.1109/45.983342 |issue=5 |bibcode=2002IPot...20e..39J }}</ref><ref name="Penney2">{{cite arXiv |last=Duda |first=Jarek |date=2008-02-24 |title=Complex base numeral systems |eprint=0712.1309 |class=math.DS }}</ref>).

==In general==
Let <math>D</math> be an [[integral domain]] <math>\subset \C</math>, and <math>|\cdot|</math> the [[Absolute value (algebra)#Types of absolute value|(Archimedean) absolute value]] on it.

A number <math>X\in D</math> in a positional number system is represented as an expansion
: <math> X = \pm \sum_{\nu}^{ } x_\nu \rho^\nu,</math>
where
:{| class="table left"
|-
| <math>\rho \in D</math> || || is the '''radix''' (or '''base''') with <math>|\rho| > 1</math>,
|-
| <math>\nu \in \Z</math> || || is the exponent (position or place),
|-
| <math>x_\nu</math> || || are digits from the ''finite'' set of digits <math>Z \subset D</math>, usually with <math>|x_\nu| < |\rho|.</math>
|}
The [[cardinality]] <math>R:=|Z|</math> is called the ''level of decomposition''.

A positional number system or '''coding system''' is a pair

: <math>\left\langle \rho, Z \right\rangle</math>

with radix <math>\rho</math> and set of digits <math>Z</math>, and we write the standard set of digits with <math>R</math> digits as

: <math>Z_R := \{0, 1, 2,\dotsc, {R-1}\}.</math>

Desirable are coding systems with the features:
* Every number in <math>D</math>, e.&nbsp;g. the integers <math>\Z</math>, the [[Gaussian integer]]s <math>\Z[\mathrm i]</math> or the integers <math>\Z[\tfrac{-1+\mathrm i\sqrt7}2]</math>, is ''uniquely'' representable as a ''finite'' code, possibly with a [[Sign (mathematics)|sign]] ±.
* Every number in the [[field of fractions]] <math>K:=\operatorname{Quot}(D)</math>, which possibly is [[Complete metric space|completed]] for the [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] given by <math>|\cdot|</math> yielding <math>K:=\R</math> or <math>K:=\C</math>, is representable as an infinite series <math>X</math> which converges under <math>|\cdot|</math> for <math>\nu \to -\infty</math>, and the [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] of the set of numbers with more than one representation is 0. The latter requires that the set <math>Z</math> be minimal, i.e. <math>R=|\rho|</math> for [[real number]]s and <math>R=|\rho|^2</math> for complex numbers.

== In the real numbers ==
In this notation our standard decimal coding scheme is denoted by
:<math>\left\langle 10, Z_{10} \right\rangle,</math>
the standard binary system is
:<math>\left\langle 2, Z_2 \right\rangle,</math>
the [[Negative base|negabinary]] system is
:<math>\left\langle -2, Z_2 \right\rangle,</math>
and the balanced ternary system<ref name="Knuth2"/> is
:<math>\left\langle 3, \{-1,0,1\} \right\rangle.</math>
All these coding systems have the mentioned features for <math>\Z</math> and <math>\R</math>, and the last two do not require a sign.

== In the complex numbers ==
Well-known positional number systems for the complex numbers include the following (<math>\mathrm i</math> being the [[imaginary unit]]):
* <math>\left\langle\sqrt{R},Z_R\right\rangle</math>, e.g. <math>\left\langle\pm \mathrm i \sqrt{2},Z_2\right\rangle</math> <ref name="Knuth1"/> and
:<math>\left\langle\pm 2\mathrm i,Z_4\right\rangle</math>,<ref name="Knuth2"/> the [[quater-imaginary base]], proposed by [[Donald Knuth]] in 1955.

* <math>\left\langle\sqrt{2}e^{\pm \tfrac{\pi}2 \mathrm i}=\pm \mathrm i\sqrt{2},Z_2\right\rangle</math> and
:<math>\left\langle\sqrt{2}e^{\pm \tfrac{3 \pi}4 \mathrm i}=-1\pm\mathrm i,Z_2\right\rangle</math><ref name="Khmelnik1"/><ref name="Penney1"/> (see also the section [[#Base_.E2.88.921_.C2.B1_i|Base −1 ± '''i''']] below).

* <math>\left\langle\sqrt{R}e^{\mathrm i\varphi},Z_R\right\rangle</math>, where <math>\varphi=\pm \arccos{(-\beta/(2\sqrt{R}))}</math>, <math>\beta<\min(R, 2\sqrt{R})</math> and <math>\beta_{ }^{ }</math> is a positive integer that can take multiple values at a given <math>R</math>.<ref name="Khmelnik2">{{cite journal |last=Khmelnik |first=S.I. |title=Positional coding of complex numbers
|journal=Questions of Radio Electronics (In Russian)|volume=XII |issue=9 |year=1966}}</ref> For <math>\beta=1</math> and <math>R=2</math> this is the system
:<math>\left\langle\tfrac{-1+\mathrm i\sqrt7}2,Z_2\right\rangle.</math>

* <math>\left\langle 2e^{\tfrac{\pi}3 \mathrm i},A_4:=\left\{0,1,e^{\tfrac{2 \pi}3 \mathrm i},e^{-\tfrac{2 \pi}3 \mathrm i}\right\}\right\rangle</math>.<ref name="Khmelnik3">{{cite book |last=Khmelnik |first=S.I. |title=Coding of Complex Numbers and Vectors (in Russian)|publisher=Mathematics in Computer |location=Israel |isbn=978-0-557-74692-7 | year=2004 |url=http://mic34.com/Magazine/94846.pdf}}</ref>
* <math>\left\langle-R,A_R^2\right\rangle</math>, where the set <math>A_R^2</math> consists of complex numbers <math>r_\nu=\alpha_\nu^1+\alpha_\nu^2\mathrm i</math>, and numbers <math>\alpha_\nu^{ } \in Z_R</math>, e.g.
:<math>\left\langle -2, \{0,1,\mathrm i,1+\mathrm i\}\right\rangle.</math><ref name="Khmelnik3"/>

* <math>\left\langle\rho=\rho_2,Z_2\right\rangle</math>, where <math>\rho_2=\begin{cases}
  (-2)^{\tfrac{\nu}2}            & \text{if } \nu \text{ even,}\\
  (-2)^{\tfrac{\nu-1}2}\mathrm i & \text{if } \nu \text{ odd.}
\end{cases}</math>&nbsp;<ref name="Khmelnik4">{{cite book |last=Khmelnik |first=S.I. |title=Method and system for processing complex numbers |url=http://worldwide.espacenet.com/publicationDetails/biblio?DB=EPODOC&adjacent=true&locale=en_EP&FT=D&date=20030814&CC=US&NR=2003154226A1&KC=A1 |publisher=Patent USA, US2003154226 (A1) |year=2001 }}</ref>

==Binary systems==
''Binary'' coding systems of complex numbers, i.e. systems with the digits <math>Z_2=\{0,1\}</math>, are of practical interest.<ref name="Khmelnik4"/>
Listed below are some coding systems <math>\langle \rho, Z_2 \rangle</math> (all are special cases of the systems above) and resp. codes for the (decimal) numbers {{math|−1, 2, −2, '''i'''}}.
The standard binary (which requires a sign, first line) and the "negabinary" systems (second line) are also listed for comparison. They do not have a genuine expansion for {{math|'''i'''}}.

As in all positional number systems with an [[Absolute value (algebra)#Types of absolute value|''Archimedean'' absolute value]], there are some numbers with [[Negative base#Non-unique representations|multiple representations]]. Examples of such numbers are shown in the right column of the table. All of them are [[repeating fraction]]s with the repetend marked by a horizontal line above it.

If the set of digits is minimal, the set of such numbers has a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] of 0. This is the case with all the mentioned coding systems.

The almost binary quater-imaginary system is listed in the bottom line for comparison purposes. There, real and imaginary part interleave each other.

==Base {{math|−1 ± i}}==
[[Image:ComplexTwindragon.svg|thumb|right|290px|The complex numbers with integer part all zeroes in the base {{math|'''i'''  – 1}} system]]
Of particular interest are the [[quater-imaginary base]] (base {{math|2'''i'''}}) and the base {{math|−1 ± '''i'''}} systems discussed below, both of which can be used to finitely represent the [[Gaussian integer]]s without sign.

Base {{math|−1 ± '''i'''}}, using digits {{math|0}} and {{math|1}}, was proposed by S. Khmelnik in 1964<ref name="Khmelnik1"/> and Walter F. Penney in 1965.<ref name="Penney0"/><ref name="Penney2"/> 

=== Connection to the twindragon ===
The rounding region of an integer – i.e., a set <math>S</math> of complex (non-integer) numbers that share the integer part of their representation in this system – has in the complex plane a fractal shape: the [[dragon curve#Twindragon|twindragon]] (see figure). This set <math>S</math> is, by definition, all points that can be written as <math>\textstyle \sum_{k\geq 1}x_k (\mathrm i-1)^{-k}</math> with <math>x_k\in Z_2</math>. <math>S</math> can be decomposed into 16 pieces congruent to <math>\tfrac14 S</math>. Notice that if <math>S</math> is rotated counterclockwise by 135°, we obtain two adjacent sets congruent to <math>\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}S</math>, because <math>(\mathrm i-1)S=S\cup(S+1)</math>. The rectangle <math>R\subset S</math> in the center intersects the coordinate axes counterclockwise at the following points: <math>\tfrac2{15}\gets 0.\overline{00001100}</math>, <math>\tfrac1{15} \mathrm i\gets 0.\overline{00000011}</math>, and <math>-\tfrac8{15}\gets 0.\overline{11000000}</math>, and <math>-\tfrac4{15} \mathrm i\gets 0.\overline{00110000}</math>. Thus, <math>S</math> contains all complex numbers with absolute value ≤{{sfrac|1|15}}.<ref>Knuth 1998 p.206</ref>

As a consequence, there is an [[Injective function|injection]] of the complex rectangle
: <math>[-\tfrac8{15},\tfrac2{15}]\times[-\tfrac4{15},\tfrac1{15}]\mathrm i</math>
into the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] <math>[0,1)</math> of real numbers by mapping
: <math>\textstyle \sum_{k\geq 1}x_k (\mathrm i-1)^{-k} \mapsto \sum_{k\geq 1}x_k b^{-k}</math>
with <math>b > 2</math>.<ref>Base <math>b = 2</math> cannot be taken because both, <math>\textstyle 2^{-1} = 0.1_{\text{bin}} = 0.5_{\text{dec}} </math> and <math>\textstyle \sum_{k\geq 2} 2^{-k} = 0.0\overline{1}_{\text{bin}} = 0.1_{\text{bin}} = 0.5_{\text{dec}}</math>. However, <math>\textstyle (\mathrm i-1)^{-1} = -0.1_{\text{bin}} -0.1_{\text{bin}} \mathrm i = -0.5_{\text{dec}} -0.5_{\text{dec}} \mathrm i</math> &nbsp; is unequal to &nbsp; <math>\textstyle \sum_{k\geq 2} (\mathrm i-1)^{-k} = 0.1_{\text{dec}} +0.3_{\text{dec}} \mathrm i </math>.</ref>

Furthermore, there are the two mappings
:<math>\begin{array}{lll}
Z_2^\N & \to & S \\
\left(x_k\right)_{k\in\N} & \mapsto & \sum_{k\geq 1}x_k (\mathrm i-1)^{-k}
\end{array}</math>
and
:<math>\begin{array}{lll}
Z_2^\N & \to & [0,1) \\
\left(x_k\right)_{k\in\N} & \mapsto & \sum_{k\geq 1}x_k 2^{-k}
\end{array}</math>
both [[surjective]], which give rise to a surjective (thus space-filling) mapping
:<math>[0,1) \qquad \to \qquad S </math>
which, however, is not [[Continuous function|continuous]] and thus ''not'' a [[space-filling curve|space-filling ''curve'']]. But a very close relative, the [[Dragon curve#Twindragon|Davis-Knuth dragon]], is continuous and a space-filling curve.
